EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After several days of precipitation across the area, skies cleared out during the evening of December 2 and early morning of December 3. The clearing skies and diminished winds resulted in the first day of the season with widespread dense fog in the San Joaquin Valley where visibility was reduced to below a quarter mile. Traffic was paced along State Route 99 between Tulare and Delano during the morning commute, and several school districts had fog related delayed openings for the first time this season. The fog lifted by late morning, and the low level moisture in the valley mixed out the following day as a another storm moved through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Madera. Visibility of 250 feet was reported on SR 41 over the San Joaquin River near Madera Ranchos.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One person was killed in a two vehicle accident near Potosi (Grant County) on the morning of April 8th. The driver of a pickup failed to stop for a stop sign at an intersection on U.S. Highway 61, collided with a semi-truck, and was thrown from the vehicle. According to the accident report, the incident occurred during dense fog. The automated weather observing equipment at the Platteville (Grant County) and Dubuque (Dubuque County) airports were both reporting dense fog with a quarter mile or less visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The driver of a pickup failed to stop for a stop sign at an intersection along U.S. Highway 61 near Potosi, collided with a semi-truck and was thrown from the vehicle. According to the accident report, the driver was pronounced dead at the scene of the accident and that dense fog was a contributing factor. The automated weather observing equipment at the Platteville and Dubuque airports were both reporting dense fog with a visibility of a quarter mile or less at the time of the accident.

The system that dropped through the Great Basin during the afternoon and evening of January 1 produced a northerly flow over the area which caused low level clouds to bank up over the southern San Joaquin Valley. This inhibited fog formation south of Fresno during the morning of January 2. However, skies remained mainly clear north of Fresno and fog formed along the State Route 99 corridor between Madera and Turlock; impacting travel along State Route 99. The fog lifted by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Merced, Atwater and Madera. Webcams showed very low visibility in Livingston and Chowchilla.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The low clouds which persisted over the southern portion of the San Joaquin Valley on January 2 pushed southward during the afternoon and evening causing low level moisture to push into the Tehachapi Mountains. This resulted in dense fog forming around Tehachapi. The fog also produced black ice as temperatures fell below freezing during the evening impacting travel along State Route 58. The fog dissipated by late evening and skies cleared out overnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Tehachapi. Webcams showed very low visibility in the Tehachapi area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dense fog which prevailed over much of the San Joaquin Valley on January 7 lifted into a stratus deck which expanded toward the valley facing slopes of the Sierra foothills and Kern County Mountains. Northerly flow resulted in the stratus banking up in the Fort Tejon and Tehachapi areas which resulted in dense fog which impacted travel over the Tejon and Tehachapi passes on January 8. Downslope wind gusts impacted the ridge tops and below the passes in Kern County Mountains during the morning hours of January 8 with several locations measuring gusts exceeding 45 mph, and a few low impact indicator sites briefly measuring gusts exceeding 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Tehachapi. Webcams showed very low visibility in the Tehachapi area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The low pressure system which moved across northern California and brought some light precipitation and gusty winds to the area on the previous day moved out of the region with high pressure building back into the area overnight. This resulted in clearing skies and diminished winds on the San Joaquin Valley and areas of dense fog subsequently formed in the valley overnight. The fog mainly impacted the south end of the San Joaquin Valley in Kern County, and the east side of the valley in Tulare County as well as a portion of Fresno County near Reedley and Sanger. The fog lifted into a low cloud deck by late morning which then slowly dissipated during the early afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Reedley. A trained spotter reported visbility of 700 feet in Sanger.

High pressure built into Southern California on April 22nd and continued through April 30th. The deserts experienced the most extreme heat, but the coast and valleys also had multiple days with record breaking heat. Palm Springs International Airport recorded 8 days with high temperatures exceeding 101 degrees, which has not occurred since April of 1945. According to San Diego County, there were 31 heat related calls placed by residents from April 24th through the 30th, with 22 of them transported to the hospital. With onshore flow and high pressure overhead, dense fog occurred at a few coastal San Diego locations on April 25th and 26th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brown Field reported 1/4 mile visibility from 0400 to 0800 PST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large area of upper level high pressure over the Southwestern U.S. generated a prolonged heatwave from May 5th - 10th. Deserts were quite hot with some records broken. The high temperatures at Palm Springs International Airport were 101 degrees or higher for seven consecutive days (May 4-10). Even coastal areas got in on the warm weather, with San Diego International Airport hitting 85 degrees on May 6th. Coastal areas of San Diego County also experienced some dense fog on the mornings of the 7th and 8th. An accompanying shortwave trough brought some elevated convection bringing locally up to one quarter of an inch of rainfall on May 9th and another shortwave trough brought some windy conditions to the mountains and deserts with gusts 55-65 miles per hour on May 12th and 13th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Areas of coastal San Diego County experienced patchy dense fog on the early mornings of May 7th and 8th. San Diego International Airport reported one quarter mile visibility on the 7th and Miramar MCAS reported a visibility near zero on the 8th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure built back into central California during the morning of November 14 as the system which brushed the area the previous day moved out of the region. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of December 21, dense fog developed over the southern Sacramento Valley and northern San Joaquin Valleys. Observation sites within in the area generally reported dense fog with visibility at or less than a quarter of a mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Boundary layer moisture remained elevated across the central deserts during the morning hours on December 11th following the passage of a wet winter storm system. As skies cleared and winds became light, the high humidity allowed for the formation of dense fog in portions of the greater Phoenix area, from the west valley southeastward and into the town of Maricopa. More than one trained spotter reported dense fog with visibility below one quarter of a mile; a spotter near the town or Maricopa reported visibility down to 100 feet as seen in a picture. Additionally, the official AWOS weather station at the Goodyear airport measured a visibility to one quarter of a mile at 0605MST. There were no reports of accidents due to the sharply reduced visibilities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Humidity in the low levels remained high following the passage of a wet Pacific weather system and as skies cleared and winds became light, conditions became favorable for the formation of dense fog. According to trained spotters across northwest Pinal County, dense fog developed during the morning hours on December 11. At 0512MST a spotter 7 miles south of Sacaton reported that visibility had fallen to 100 yards or less in dense fog. Later in the morning at 0856MST, another spotter located 1 mile west of the town of Maricopa reported visibility down to 100 feet as seen in a photo taken by the spotter. A Dense Fog Advisory had been issued at 0505MST and was in effect at the time of the dense fog reports. There were no reports of accidents due to the sharply reduced visibility.

Following the departure of the slow moving low pressure system which brought low elevation snowfall to portions of central California and disrupted holiday travel on December 29 and 30, upslope flow over the Tehachapi Mountains resulted in low clouds banking up producing dense fog in the Tehachapi Valley and to the north of Tejon Pass along interstate 5 which further disrupted holiday travelers during the evening of December 30 until the early afternoon of December 31.  In addition, areas of dense fog formed for a few hours in the San Joaquin Valley where skies cleared out, disrupting travel along SR 99 during the morning of December 31 until the fog lifted into a low cloud deck.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Hanford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front pushed through central California during the afternoon of November 4.  Behind the front, upslope clouds persisted overnight and through the morning of November 5 along the Sierra foothills and the valley facing slopes of the Tehachapi Mountains.  Some of the upslope moisture banked up in the Tehachapi area resulting in a short period (between an hour and an hour and a half) of dense fog which resulted in visibility lowering to below 1000 feet in Tehachapi.  The fog lifted into a low cloud deck then mixed out by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Tehachapi.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following widespread 1 to 2 inches of rain on Christmas Eve, dense fog developed in parts of the Greater Phoenix Area in the morning of Christmas Day, particularly in the southwest and far southeast parts of the metro. No reports of ground traffic being impacted were found. The fog was considered significant seeing as it is a once, maybe twice, a year occurrence in the Phoenix area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Chandler Municipal Airport and Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport both reported visibilities down to or below a quarter of a mile from 0547MST to 0950MST. There were also multiple photos and videos from this area showing visibilities down to a few hundred feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dense fog was a factor in a several car accident in Kaufman County that resulted in a total of 13 injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first accident occurred shortly before 7:00 this morning on US 175 and SH 274 in Kemp with a semi and two cars. There were 2 injuries at that incident. Approximately 3-4 minutes later there was an accident at US 175 and Business 175 in Kemp with two cars and no injuries. Then there was an accident involving 3-4 vehicles at US 175 east of FM 2860 (between Jiba and Kemp), and moments later one on US 175 just west of FM 2860 involving 4-5 vehicles. The two at FM 2860 had a total of 7 injured with 3 being transported by ambulance. The weather conditions were dense fog with visibility below 300 feet in the area along US 175 described above, with visibility below 100 feet in several locations along and either side of US 175 up to a mile from the highway.

High pressure rebuilt over central California during the early morning of January 11.  As a result of mainly clear skies, light winds and inversion conditions over the San Joaquin Valley, areas of dense fog formed overnight south of Fresno.  The fog persisted until late morning in some locations and travel was impacted on several state highways in the impacted area with California Highway Patrol pacing traffic.  In addition, several school  districts opened late and further delayed or cancelled bus service due to the fog.  By late morning the fog had lifted into a low cloud deck which dissipated during the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Hanford. Several webcams showed visibility below 1000 feet. Several school districts either opened late or delayed or cancelled bus service.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A multiple vehicle accident occurred on Jewel Crowe Road near Blue Springs in Worth County due to dense fog around 7:05 am. When the Battalion Chief arrived on scene, he radioed out for all incoming response to use caution as there was zero visibility. The accident scene at Jewel Crowe was in a section of the road that dips down near the creek. This was a 5 vehicle accident that involved a school bus. There were 4 students on the bus that had minor injuries and were transported to local hospitals/doctors by their parents to be examined. There were two fatalities. Both fatalities were the female drivers of two separate vehicles involved. Those 2 vehicles did have a head on collision.  In one of those vehicles there were 2 passengers:  a 16 year old female that was transported by helicopter to Macon in critical condition.  The other passenger was a baby that had no injuries. The last two vehicles involved were both trucks, and those drivers were male and were out of their vehicles with no apparent injuries when personnel arrived on scene. Another Worth County School bus came upon the accident site and was barely able to keep from colliding with the other 5 vehicles because of the limited visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A localized superfog event occurred along Interstate 95 near Edgewater in Volusia County. Residual smoke from a nearby prescribed burn from the previous day combined with fog to create near-zero visibility conditions. This resulted in five separate accidents on both travel lanes of the Interstate that involved 17 vehicles at, and just south of mile marker 244. There were three fatalities and 10 injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Florida Highway Patrol (FHP) reported five (5) separate accidents involving 17 vehicles on Interstate 95 at or just south of mile marker 244 (near State Road 442) at approximately 0130LST. In total there were three fatalities and 10 injuries as a result of these crashes. In the northbound lanes, four separate crashes occurred involving 11 vehicles, resulting in one fatality. In the southbound lanes, there was one crash involving six vehicles - one SUV, one van, and four tractor trailers. There were two fatalities, one being the driver of the SUV and the other a driver of one of the tractor trailers. Several people were trapped in their vehicles and had to be extricated. A child was airlifted to Orlando Health Arnold Palmer Hospital for Children in stable condition, and nine other victims were taken to the Halifax Health Medical Center in Daytona Beach with non-life-threatening injuries. An 18 mile stretch of Interstate 95 was closed for most of the day from State Road 44 in Volusia County (near Edgewater) to County Road 5A in Brevard County (near Scottsmoor). Two tractor trailers that collided in the southbound lanes caught on fire, which resulted in extensive damage to the roadway that had to be repaved before reopening to traffic.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dense fog along portions of Interstate 57 between the Mississippi River and Interstate 55 resulted in several fatalities (indirect) in a massive pile-up. The pile-up occurred on both sides of the interstate near Charleston, Missouri in Mississippi County. Approximately 50  vehicles were involved, including multiple tractor trailer rigs. Several vehicles erupted into flames. The visibility was below one-quarter mile at the closest automated airport observing site at Sikeston, Missouri. First responders at the scene reported visibility was around 50 feet. The first collision occurred when a semi tractor-trailer rear-ended another semi at the 13.4 mile marker southbound near Charleston. That accident caused a pile-up that included 15 vehicles. Two people were seriously injured, and two others received minor injuries. A second collision occurred almost simultaneously on the northbound side of the interstate, caused by the collision in the southbound lanes. A total of 14 people were injured, six seriously. High pressure built into central California during the early morning of November 10 as the large upper trough which brought widespread precipitation to the area the previous three days moved east of the area. This allowed for skies to clear out and winds to diminish resulting in areas of dense fog forming in the San Joaquin Valley toward daybreak. The fog was most noticeable in Madera where traffic along SR 99 was impacted.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Madera.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High clouds moving over the area during the morning of November 11 inhibited dense fog from forming in the San Joaquin Valley, but the clouds moved out of the area overnight and skies had cleared out by the morning of November 12. With light winds and inversion condition present, a narrow strip of dense fog formed by daybreak along SR 99 between Tulare and Selma where visibility was reduced to a few hundred feet and traffic was impacted along SR 99 for a few hours until the fog burned off.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Hanford. Several webcams showed visibility below 1000 feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clear skies and light winds along with strong radiational cooling and a low level inversion made for favorable conditions for areas of dense fog to form by daybreak. Several webcams showed visibility below 1000 feet in Madera and Merced Counties where several school districts opened late for the first time this season due to dense fog. Patches of dense fog were also prevalent during the morning hours further south in Selma and Hanford. The fog completely dissipated by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Atwater, Merced and Madera. Several webcams showed visibility below 1000 feet. Several school districts opened late because of dense fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple days of dense fog combined with below freezing temperatures led to heavy frost and ice forming on power lines over northwest into parts of north central North Dakota. The greatest damage occurred over the far northwest where nearly 60 power poles were broken, with additional poles broken over parts of  north central North Dakota. Multiple lines and cross-arms were also damaged or broken. At least 500 customers suffered power losses, some for multiple days. Over southwest North Dakota in Stark County, near zero visibility due to dense fog led to one indirect death. According to the North Dakota Highway Patrol, a semi-truck jackknifed while traveling along Interstate 94 during the very early morning hours of January 16, with the trailer blocking the westbound passing lane. A 50 year old female from Dickinson, also traveling westbound, died (indirect) when she hit the trailer on the left-rear side and went under it.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dense fog developed during the afternoon of January 15, continuing through much of the day of January 16. At 2:30 AM CST on January 16, a semi-truck traveling westbound on Interstate 94 eleven miles east of Dickinson lost control and jackknifed into the median, with the trailer blocking the westbound passing lane. A 50 year old female from Dickinson, also traveling westbound, died (indirect) when she hit the trailer on the left-rear side and went under it.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Typical radiation fog forms when the surface quickly cools at night to become nearly saturated and can become dense when conditions trap more moisture near the surface, usually in the presence of high pressure as what was observed on 10/23. Super fog forms when a mixture of smoke and moisture released from damp smoldering organic material such as brush, leaves and trees, mixes with cooler, nearly saturated air or fog. Ongoing drought conditions set the stage for marsh fires caused by an unknown reason  to develop and persist. Smoke from fires located near New Orleans East and Lafitte was trapped near the surface due to a strong temperature inversion that is typically present in fog setups. Smoke gradually spread westward during the morning hours due to the light easterly winds. This combo of smoke and fog conditions led to superfog over I-55 during the morning commute. A chain reaction event of car accidents occurred on I-55 near mile marker 14 due to the superfog. There were dozens of injuries and 7 fatalities.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A chain reaction event of car accidents occurred on I-55 near mile marker 14 as dense fog reduced visibility to near zero. The pile up that took place included 158 vehicles and resulted in dozens of injuries and several fatalities. Many vehicles caught fire and one toppled over the interstate guard rail and ended up in Lake Maurepas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upslope winds during the morning of November 19 resulted in some locally dense fog in he southeastern portion of the San Joaquin Valley. This was most noticeable in the Porterville area where visibility remained below a quarter mile for a part of the early morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clearing skies and light winds over the San Joaquin Valley during the morning of November 17 allowed for areas of dense fog to form by daybreak as some low level moisture remained as a result of the system which moved through the area two days before. This was the first widespread dense fog event in the area as visibility was reduced to an eighth of a mile or less at several locations, and several school districts either opened late or delayed bus service for the first time this season as a result of the fog. The fog dissipated by late morning as another incoming system provided for some mixing to take place.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility below a quarter mile was reported in Merced and Madera. Several webcams showed visibility below 1000 feet. Several school districts opened late because of dense fog.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cloud layer forming from upslope processes along the Blue Mountain Foothills resulted in ground fog developing between Cabbage Hill and Poverty Flats in the Northern Blue mountains, or between at least mile posts 219 and 229 along I-84. Reductions in visibilities lead to a significant multi-vehicle accident that closed the freeway down for approximately 8 hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around 12:30pm PDT, Oregon State Patrol responded to an multi-vehicle incident involving nearly 30 vehicles near mile post 227 on I-84, with two confirmed semi-trucks having caught fire, several motorists reporting minor injuries, and at least one report of a series injury. Multiple Oregon DOT weather stations between mileposts 219 and 229 reported visibilities a quarter mile or less at times before and after the traffic incident. Due to the incident, I-84 was closed both directions between Pendleton and La Grande for over 8 hours according to media.

A semi-truck failed to move over for vehicles responding to an earlier accident, and while attempting to avoid collision, rolled over and crushed a fire-rescue vehicle and hit an ambulance resulting in several (indirect) minor injuries.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Areas of dense fog resulted in mist and drizzle in southeast Minnesota on December 16th. Automated weather observation stations reported above freezing surface temperatures and minimum visibilities of 1/4 statute miles at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minnesota State Patrol reported an automobile accident along Minnesota State Highway 14 in Claremont Township on the afternoon of December 16th. Nearby automated weather observation stations reported rain, mist, and dense fog through much of the day. The accident report filed by the Minnesota State Patrol on December 16th classified the road conditions as wet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure led to stable conditions and cold pool formation across the Northern Rockies. This led to a prolonged period of dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dense fog formed at the Missoula International Airport around 22:25 MST on December 15, with visibility below one quarter statute mile. Visibility briefly improved to one half mile between 11:53 MST and 15:30 MST on December 16, before returning to one quarter mile after 15:30. Dense fog lasted through 0910 MST on December 17, with visibility continuing to move between one half mile and one quarter mile through 0625 MST on December 18. In total, Missoula International Airport was below airport landing minimums for around 28 hours. This led to multiple days of flight delays, cancellations, and diversions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A small plane with four people onboard crashed near Moss Beach in San Mateo County, around 1 mile southwest of Half Moon Bay Airport, on January 14 at 7:34 PM. Witnesses saw the plane sputtering before the crash. Wreckage from the plane was found near Ross Cove. Search efforts for survivors continued until 11 AM the next day. The San Mateo County Sheriff's Office stated that a commercial fishing boat discovered a woman's body in the water. The body was later identified to be connected to the crash.||At the time of the accident, Half Moon Bay Airport reported scattered low ceilings and misty skies. The last observation before the incident reported scattered clouds at 300 feet and visibilities at 6 miles. Separate observations from the previous two hours reported broken clouds at 300 feet and visibilities of 2.5 miles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small plane with four people onboard crashed near Moss Beach in San Mateo County, around 1 mile southwest of Half Moon Bay Airport, on January 14 at 7:34 PM. Witnesses saw the plane sputtering before the crash. Wreckage from the plane was found near Ross Cove. Search efforts for survivors continued until 11 AM the next day. The San Mateo County Sheriff's Office stated that a commercial fishing boat discovered a woman's body in the water. The body was later identified to be connected to the crash.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure moved into central California on January 17 which resulted in clearing skies and light winds over the area by the evening. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As several weak systems moved through the area during the last week of 2024, they helped to create pools of rich moisture trapped in the lower elevation valleys. These pools of moisture condensed during the overnight period into widespread areas of dense fog. The lower elevation river valleys of eastern Utah and western Colorado were mainly effected.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At around 2:30AM local time, the KCNY ASOS at Canyonlands Airport, about 10 miles north of Moab, UT, began reporting visibility reduced to 1/4 mile or less. In addition, satellite imagery indicated that the dense fog was widespread throughout the zone, particularly along well travelled highway corridors. As the sun rose, road cameras provided by the Utah Department of Transportation allowed for visual confirmation of the extent of the fog. This fog lingered through the morning before beginning to finally lift around 12PM local time. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: While drier air moving in to the region began to scour out the rich pockets of low level moisture across the lower elevation valleys of eastern Utah and western Colorado, deep moisture lingered in the eastern Uinta Basin. This moisture condensed during the overnight hours, creating dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At approximately 6:45AM local time, the KVEL ASOS at Vernal Airport, in Vernal, UT began reporting visibilities of 1/4 mile or less. Additionally, satellite imagery helped to confirm that the dense fog was more than just localized at the airport. As the sun rose, road cameras provided by the Utah Department of Transportation added visual conformation of the extent of the dense fog, particularly along the US Highway 40 corridor. This fog lingered into the morning before beginning to lift after 10AM local time, as dry air and sunshine began to erode the surface moisture. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

Unsettled conditions at the end of December brought widespread precipitation to the region. This precipitation, in the form of both rain and snow, allowed for pockets of rich low level moisture to settle into valley locations. As skies cleared in the wake of each passing upper level wave, this rich moisture condensed into areas of dense fog, with several locations reporting visibilities of a quarter mile or less.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The K4V0 AWOS in Rangely, CO reported visibilities of less than 1/2 mile beginning around 6 AM local time. In addition, satellite imagery indicated widespread areas of dense fog similar to that around Rangely throughout the Lower Yampa River Basin. As the sun began to rise, a camera located at Rangely Airport, provided by the Federal Aviation Administration, as well as road cameras provided by the Colorado Department of Transportation, allowed for visual confirmation of dense fog. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

As moisture began to increase ahead of an atmospheric river fueled winter storm, areas of dense fog developed along the central and upper Yampa River basin in northwestern Colorado. While impacts were minimal, this fog was widespread and long-lasting, reducing visibility along the US Highway 40 corridor to less than 1/4 miles in places.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread fog was spotted across the upper and central Yampa river valley via a combination of Colorado Department of Transportation cameras, satellite data, and ASOS and AWOS visibilities. Visibility at the KCAG ASOS at Craig-Moffat County Airport was reduced to 1/4 mile or less for several hours. No reports of damages or injuries were received as a result of fog on this morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong, moist winter storm had moved through eastern Utah and western Colorado in the days prior to this dense fog event. Accumulating snow had made it down the floor of the Grand Valley, particularly in areas west of Fruita toward the Utah border. With warm air advection aloft and moisture and cold surface temperatures, the development of dense fog was favored on the morning of the 27th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Patchy dense fog developed through the morning of November 27th across the Grand Valley, mainly west of Grand Junction and into eastern Utah along I-70. The KGJT ASOS at the Grand Junction Regional Airport reported visibility of 1/4 mile during this event. Additionally, Colorado Department of Transportation cameras along I-70 showed areas of dense fog with less than a 1/4 mile visibility in areas around the Rabbit Valley exit, and satellite imagery in combination with Utah Department of Transportation cameras indicated areas of dense fog stretched as far west at Cisco, UT. No reports of damages or injuries were received in conjunction with this fog event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days after a winter storm that brought accumulating snow to the northwest Colorado valleys, skies cleared and nighttime temperatures dropped off. This allowed trapped low level moisture,  supplemented by the fresh snowfall, to condense into dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at Craig-Moffat County Airport (KCAG) reported dense fog conditions with visibility under 1/4 for two hours during this period, while the KHDN AWOS at Yampa Valley Airport was in and out of dense fog during this period. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the days after a winter storm that brought accumulating snow to the northwest Colorado valleys, skies cleared and nighttime temperatures dropped off. This allowed trapped low level moisture,  supplemented by the fresh snowfall, to condense into dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dense fog with visibilities less than 1/2 mile were recorded periodically at the KCAG ASOS at Craig-Moffat County airport, with most of the period seeing visibility ranging between 3/4 mile and 1 mile. The KHDN AWOS at Yampa Valley Airport reported dense fog with visibility less than 1/4 mile through much of the day on the 7th, with a brief period of improved conditions after 9PM local time. With clear skies, light winds and inversion conditions present during the morning hours, an area of dense fog developed in the central portion of the San Joaquin Valley which impacted travel along the SR 198 corridor and along portions of SR 99 in Tulare County during the morning commute. There were also patches of short lived dense fog elsewhere in the San Joaquin Valley. The fog lifted into a low cloud deck not long after sunrise and completely dissipated by late morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Visibility of one eighth of a mile was reported in Hanford. Webcams indicated visibility below 1000 feet in Hanford.

A wet spring storm had moved through western Colorado in the days before this event, bringing mountain snow, as well as mixed rain and snow in the lower elevation valleys. Particularly, in the southern Colorado valleys, rain and snow allowed for increased surface moisture to become trapped. As skies cleared and temperatures cooled, this trapped moisture condensed, becoming patchy dense fog across the southwestern Colorado valleys.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: According to the KDRO ASOS in Durango, dense fog developed at the airport around 1:15 AM local time, with visibility rapidly dropping to 1/4 mile or less. The KDRO ASOS continued to report this very low visibility through approximately 7:30 AM local time, at which point visibility began to gradually improve. The fog had fully lifted by 9:00AM local time. Satellite imagery also indicated this area of dense fog stretching along the lower elevations of the zone, close to the New Mexico border, and extending into neighboring forecast zones. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received in association with this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wet spring storm had moved through western Colorado in the days before this event, bringing mountain snow, as well as mixed rain and snow in the lower elevation valleys. Particularly, in the southern Colorado valleys, rain and snow allowed for increased surface moisture to become trapped. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dense fog that produced visibility of 1/4 mile or less at the KDRO ASOS was observed, via satellite, to extend into the adjacent Colorado Forecast Zone 023. The nearest surface observation points in this zone, including the KPSO AWOS, were well north of the patch of dense fog, which had remained in the river basin close to the New Mexico border. However, with the visibilities produced in the adjacent zone, it is highly likely that these conditions extended, at least locally, into this zone as well. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received related to this event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Remnants of Tropical Storm Priscilla brought record-breaking moisture and widespread precipitation to western Colorado on October 10th and 11th. Portions of the region saturated under heavy rainfall with many locations experiencing periodic drops in visibility due to mist beginning early in the morning on the 10th and persisting into the early afternoon on the 11th. Dense fog was also able to develop overnight across the Grand Valley and in lower valleys along the I-70 corridor.

The KGJT ASOS would report dense fog reducing visibility to 1/4 mile for about a half an hour shortly before midnight. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure aloft with an inversion layer persisted since the last week of November. Low temperatures dipped into the mid 30s at times when the low clouds cleared in the Central Valley. Otherwise, low temperatures were only slightly cooler when the low clouds, rather than fog, lingered. Patchy dense fog occurred at times during the first five days of the month in the San Joaquin Valley, but lifted to a stratus deck for the next few days. Dense fog was prevalent in the foothill areas, including the Grapevine, the Sierra Nevada foothills, and the coastal ranges at elevations between 1,000 feet and 2,500 feet from the 1st until the 9th.||Elsewhere, seasonably cool temperatures were recorded while dry conditions were present, such as in the mountains above 2,500 feet and the Kern County desert. Freezing overnight low temperatures were reported in the desert during the first several days of the month, which is common during December.||Fog and low stratus cloud cover continued over the San Joaquin Valley, as well as the lower Sierra Nevada foothills and coastal ranges up to around 2,500 feet for much of the second week of the month. However, dense fog became most prevalent in the San Joaquin Valley each night and morning from the 12th until the 15th. Most locations in the valley observed dense fog, even when they did not observe any clearing during the daytime on the 12th until the 15th. Enough moisture remained trapped in the Central Valley while the inversion layer served as a lid over the mountains and foothills due to the stagnant high pressure pattern in place.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CHP reports dense fog on the Grapevine portion of I-5.

No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

At approximately 4 am on November 5th, very localized dense superfog developed near a low lying creek valley along I-49 at mile marker 162 near the intersection of Highway 177 in extreme Southeast Desoto Parish. There were multiple nearby controlled burns around the area for the preceding few days that potentially could have contributed to the extremely dense and localized fog in that location. This created zero visibility, contributing to an 18 wheeler rollover in the northbound lane of I-49. Multiple other vehicles were involved in a chain reaction accident, with multiple crashes also occurring in the southbound lane at this same location. The deputies on scene described the visibility reduction where the accidents occurred as an abrupt wall of fog that was very localized. A 50 year-old male was killed, and one other person was injured from this accident. While the southbound lane of I-49 was closed only briefly during the morning, the northbound lane was closed for approximately 12 hours.

A drying atmosphere was established over western Colorado underneath high pressure ahead of a shortwave trough. Reduced visibility from mist and fog was exhibited in the nights prior, but cooler overnight low temperatures led to dense fog development and 1/4-mile visibility overnight from December 4-5.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak southwesterly flow around a deepening trough brought mid-level moisture over eastern Utah, prompting snow showers to portions of the region overnight from January 7 to 8. Breaks in cloud cover enabled enough radiational cooling to saturate some locations overnight, and localized dense fog was able to develop as a result.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed on the northern slopes of the Uintah Mountains on the morning of January 8. The K40U AWOS at the Manila Airport reported a brief period of 1/4-mile visibility due to freezing fog. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad trough moved through the CONUS in mid-January with weak flow situated over Colorado. Embedded shortwaves moved through the trough, bringing bouts of active weather, including overnight from January 8 to 9. Strong snow bands developed ahead of the cold front moving through southwestern Colorado. As skies cleared and temperatures dropped behind the front, dense fog developed within some valleys near the San Juan mountains where heavy snow had occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread fog, including areas of dense fog, developed within the Animas River Basin during the morning of January 9 following heavy snowfall. The KDRO ASOS at the Durango La-Plata County Airport reported two prolonged periods of visibility being reduced to or below 1 mile. During the first period, sporadic and brief periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog occurred. During the second period which began shortly before sunrise, dense fog reduced visibility to or less than 1/4 mile for about three and a half hours before slowly dissipating through mid-morning. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Relatively clear early-day skies on February 12 led to isolated convection with rain and snow showers across portions of western Colorado. Some valleys were already saturated or near-saturated due to periods of precipitation over the prior days. As such, in spite of dense cloud cover lingering overnight and lacking radiational cooling, saturated surface conditions paired with weakening winds were capable of producing areas of dense fog on the morning on February 13.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread dense fog developed within the Yampa River Basin during the morning of February 13. The KCAG ASOS at the Craig-Moffat County Airport reported two prolonged periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog and freezing fog, once before sunrise and once after. Several hours of reduced visibility above 1/4 mile due to mist and fog were also observed during the morning. The KEEO ASOS at the Meeker Coulter Field Airport observed almost three hours of 1/4-mile visibility due to freezing fog prior to sunrise. The KHDN AWOS at the Yampa Valley Regional Airport also reported several prolonged periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog and freezing fog both before and after sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak remnants of an atmospheric river arrived to the Four Corners region during the afternoon of February 11 and overnight into the morning of February 12. Primarily virga showers dominated as the plume of moisture first arrived. Surface moisture eventually caught up near the Abajo Mountains around midnight and coinciding with brief rain showers. The mid-level atmosphere dried out again prior to sunrise, promoting radiational cooling amidst clearing skies and the development of sparse, yet dense fog.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief and localized dense fog developed near the Abajo mountains during the early morning period of February 12. The KU64 AWOS at the Monticello Airport reported about one hour of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following multiple days of rain and snow showers, drier northwesterly flow on the backside of a shortwave trough brought clearer skies on the evening of February 13 into the morning of February 14. With ample surface moisture still in place from the prior days' precipitation and strong radiational cooling from clear skies, dense fog developed across many valleys.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed within the eastern Uinta basin during the morning of February 14. The KVEL ASOS at the Vernal Regional Airport reported two roughly 15-minute periods of 1/4-mile visibility due to freezing fog prior to sunrise. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over May 29 and 30, a shortwave trough brought light rain to numerous parts of the Intermountain West. Surface conditions remained unsaturated in spite of this, but portions of northern Colorado saw moisture linger into the morning of May 31. With this, as temperatures cooled and winds weakened overnight, the environment supported brief dense fog development within the Yampa River Basin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed within the Central Yampa River Basin during the morning of May 31. The KCAG ASOS at the Craig-Moffat County Airport reported a brief period spanning less than ten minutes of 1/4-mile visibility due to dense fog. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Relatively clear early-day skies on February 12 led to isolated convection with rain and snow showers across portions of eastern Utah. Some valleys were already saturated or near-saturated due to periods of precipitation over the prior days. As such, in spite of dense cloud cover lingering overnight and lacking radiational cooling, saturated surface conditions paired with weakening winds were capable of producing areas of dense fog on the morning on February 13.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Localized dense fog developed near the eastern Uinta Mountains during the early morning of February 13. The K40U AWOS at the Manilla Airport observed reduced visibility to 1/4 mile for about twenty minutes. No reports of injuries, damages, or fatalities were received.
